about: Where the design discussion of modular services happens. `sync.py` reads this file and nothing else; see README.md for what each `kind` means and how to add a source.

sources.why: The tracking issue. The manual points contributors at it for gaps in the infrastructure, so it collects the requirements nobody has met yet.
The pull request that landed the subsystem. Its review thread is the longest argument on record about the shape of the portable layer.
The 2023 proof of concept that preceded the merged design. Read for what was tried and dropped.
The 2017 issue asking for a service abstraction layer. The oldest statement of the problem this subsystem answers.
RFC 163. Closed, and its intermediate outcome -- try a module-based approach -- is the premise this repository works from, so the objections in it are still live.
Contracts: the competing/complementary answer to how services compose. Meetings keep returning to how the two relate.
More granular control over the system. Adjacent design space -- what a configuration framework owns versus what a service does.
Backend-agnostic secret management. Secrets are the open question a portable service cannot answer on its own.
The earlier secrets RFC, for the history behind RFC 201.
The `nixos/artifacts` implementation of RFC 201. The most-cited untracked link in the corpus: a modular service that needs a secret has nowhere portable to get one, and this is the current answer.
Contract for files containing secrets. The contracts side of the same question.
The 2017 issue on storing secrets outside the store. Everything since restates it.
Private files in the Nix store, from the Nix side. The constraint that makes the secrets question hard rather than tedious.
One way to do other types of services -- the sketch that came out of the 2017 abstraction-layer issue.
The NixOS systemd abstraction does not handle template units. A concrete limit any portable description inherits.
NixOS always imports all modules. Why a service that is *only* a module costs something.
NixOS a la carte: an earlier attempt at making the module set separable.
Replacing systemd with OpenRC or runit. The user-facing form of the demand.
When a service module should configure nginx. The reverse-proxy case is where service-to-service composition first bites.
A modular service written by someone outside the design, which is the useful kind of evidence.
RFC 42, freeform `settings`. The direct ancestor of `configData`.
RFC 78, system-agnostic configuration file generators. Same portability goal, one layer down.
Contracts across nodes, from the project contracts came from. The meetings raise the same question about services on separate machines.
The vars secrets provider, for how contracts and vars were reconciled in practice.

sources.q: repo:NixOS/nixpkgs label:"6.topic: module system" is:issue is:open
sources.why: Adjacent, not tracked: modular services are built on the module system, so its open issues bound what the design can do. Six hundred items is too many to carry, so this records the list in state/queries.json for triage instead of fetching it.
Search has to render the options before anyone can find a modular service. What it cannot index is a statement about the interface.
The indexing work itself, including the base/environment split it had to model.
The Modular Services / Package Configuration Modules board. It is the only place the work is ordered and given a status, which no issue query recovers.

The working pad: the agenda of the next meeting and the minutes of every past one, written live. It runs ahead of the Discourse posts, and it is where the link list at the top named most of the other sources here.
Auto-expanding: the meeting minutes are posted to Discourse one topic per meeting, so a title match picks up meeting N+1 without anyone editing this file.
Should we expose the type for modular services -- a direct interface question.
A service runner built against the spec from outside Nix. The clearest test of whether the description is really framework-independent.
Init system freedom on NixOS. The demand that makes a portable service description worth having, argued at length by people who want it for other reasons.
Pre-RFC: decouple services using structured typing. The ancestor of contracts.
Portable submodules: the module-system mechanism the whole approach rests on.
The finix announcement thread, where a framework that is not NixOS states what it needs from a service description.
Restructuring NixOS to work without systemd. The long-running background thread; most objections raised later appear here first.
Self Host Blocks, where the contracts work came from.
Vars: a framework for managing secrets and computed values. The most-cited untracked link of all; the meetings treat it as the likely answer for secrets.
The Discourse thread for RFC 163, where the RFC was argued outside the pull request.
Conventions for service modules? -- an open question about the very interface this repository documents.
Secrets don't belong in config. The argument behind the secrets work, stated for a general audience.
sixos: a NixOS without systemd. Another framework with its own answer, and a critic of this one.
Nixifying Kubernetes. The meetings keep citing k8s for how it wants services declared separately so it can tell what failed.

The day-to-day channel, and the only source here that needs a credential: reading any room requires an account, since matrix.nixos.org has guest access and registration disabled and the Matrix Public Archive was discontinued. The room itself sets history_visibility to world_readable and its join rule to public, so its operators have made the history readable to anyone who asks; the account is a formality of the protocol rather than a permission. A run without MATRIX_TOKEN skips this and says so.

unfetched.why: Code under discussion, not discussion. Cited from the pad; fetch the diff from git when it matters.
As above: a proposal carried as a branch rather than as a pull request, so it has no thread to fetch.
Out-of-tree experiments named in the meetings. Neither carries issues yet; add a github-query here when one does.

ignore_why: Seen often enough to crowd the triage list, and not about this design. The `actions/checkout` refs come from this repository's own Dependabot pull requests; nixpkgs#77858 is a dracut issue quoted inside a diff hunk in RFC 157; the Discourse topics are the review queues, the breaking-changes announcement, the community calendar and a hackathon report.
